bio.en: Tobi Lutke is the co-founder and CEO of Shopify, one of the most respected operator-founders in tech, known for first-principles, infinite-game thinking.
bio.zh: Tobi Lutke 是 Shopify 的联合创始人兼 CEO，是科技圈最受尊敬、以“运营者—创始人”著称的人物之一，以其第一性原理、无限游戏式的思维闻名。

summary.en: Tobi shares his leadership playbook: thinking from first principles, treating business as an infinite game, and maximizing leverage by using the best tools and agents available. He discusses why craft, simplicity, and developer happiness matter, and how he approaches strategy and hiring at Shopify's scale. The episode is a masterclass in founder-led, conviction-driven operating.
summary.zh: Tobi 分享了他的领导手册：从第一性原理思考、把商业当作无限游戏、并通过使用最佳工具与智能体来最大化杠杆。他讨论了为什么工艺、简洁与开发者的快乐至关重要，以及他在 Shopify 这种规模下如何处理战略与招聘。本期是一堂关于创始人驱动、凭信念运作的大师课。

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: Your podcast is a podcast by a builder for other builders. Here's the most interesting question I think people can ask builders, what is your energy source? My energy source is dissatisfaction with status quo. There are so many books are about this ... Technology leading to dystopia. Like no one who really thinks about this would want to be born into a world 20 years before today. I think today is the dystopia of the future. It behooves us to try to build the kinds of products that leads in ... Towards progress.
turns.zh: 你的播客是为建筑师打造的播客。以下是我认为人们可以向建筑师提出的最有趣的问题：你的能量源泉是什么？我的能量源泉是对现状的不满。市面上有太多书籍探讨这个话题……科技正将世界引向反乌托邦。没有人会真心希望出生在20年前的世界。我认为当下就是未来的反乌托邦。我们有责任努力打造能推动进步的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple quotes along these lines I've seen that describe the way you think about this stuff. "If most people are doing it a certain way I by default don't want to do it that way."
turns.zh: 我曾看到过几条类似的引语，描述了你看待这些事物的视角。“如果大多数人都在以某种方式做事，我默认就不会那样做。”

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: There's an aesthetic in the world that exists which is that business people dress in suit and tie, they are speaking much more sophisticated than I do, usually without an accent. They usually have a stick and show dramatically at the chart that is behind them. How much is that aesthetic overlapped with outperformance? Pessimism sounds extremely sophisticated. Optimism always sounds dumb or at least naive. The most powerful unquantifiable things in the word of business are fun and delight.
turns.zh: 世界上存在一种审美规范：商界人士身着西装打着领带，言辞比我要精致得多，而且通常没有口音。他们手持教鞭，戏剧性地展示身后的大屏幕图表。这种审美与卓越表现有多少重叠呢？悲观主义听起来极其高深。乐观主义总是显得愚蠢或至少天真。在商业世界中，最强大的不可量化的因素是乐趣和愉悦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know of any other company that operates where the founder has this 100-year vision of where the product needs to go and working backwards from that.
turns.zh: 我不知道还有哪家公司是以创始人对产品未来100年发展方向的百年愿景为指导，并从此倒推战略的。

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: I talk about look in the future and then think backwards a lot, right? It's like what would we want to have done 20 years ago on this? We have very long-term plans. At 100 years you can't talk about this software project but you can talk about the mission itself, whatever things that will survive for 80 years that are left on this particular timeframe. Entrepreneurship is just precious. Shopify exists, basically, to make entrepreneurship more common.
turns.zh: 我经常谈到先展望未来，再回看过去，对吧？比如20年前我们希望拥有什么？我们制定的是长期计划。谈论软件项目时，你无法谈论100年后的事情，但你可以谈论使命本身，以及在特定时间段内能存续80年的事物。创业精神无比珍贵。Shopify的存在，本质上是为了让创业更普及。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you want to leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 你有什么想留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: I really, really, really think that there is not a single person on this planet who is even close to being at their maximum potential. Reminding people of their own potential constantly is actually a wonderful thing to do.
turns.zh: 我真心、真心、真心认为，这个星球上没有一个人能充分发挥出自己的潜力。不断提醒人们意识到自身的潜力，其实是一件很棒的事情。

turns.en: I'm glad to be here. I'm excited for our conversation.
turns.zh: 很高兴能来。我对我们的对话很期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've listened to so many of your other interviews, I've talked to a bunch of people that work for you. I want to try to do something a little different. There's basically two themes that emerged over and over and over as I've listened to you share advice, and interview, and in talking to people that work for you. One is thinking from first principles, the other is maximizing human potential. I'm just going to plant these seeds for now. I'm going to not ask about these directly, I'm going to come at these from the side with the many questions that I have for you. Something that I've heard people describe at Shopify called the Tobi tornado.
turns.zh: 我听过您很多其他采访，也和您团队的很多人交流过。我想尝试一些不同的东西。在听您分享建议、接受采访以及与您团队成员交流的过程中，有两个主题反复出现。一是从第一性原理思考，另一个是最大化人类潜能。我现在先抛出这些种子，暂时不直接问这些问题，而是从侧面入手，结合我对您的诸多疑问来探讨。Shopify内部有人把您称为托比龙卷风。

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: Oh, wow. Okay, that's a start. I like it.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。好的，这是一个开始。我喜欢这个说法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the Tobi tornado?
turns.zh: 什么是托比龙卷风？

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: A Tobi tornado, I would say, is a whole lot of change management or a conversation or conflict or real talk compressed into a very short timeframe. I see something it doesn't ... It's not good, I have a conversation. I have learned something very quickly about hey, I need to update my priors, or cool, let's do it differently. At which point a project might be stopped and we get back together in a room and then we start a new version of a product. And everyone who's currently on the team, of that particular project, is no longer on the project but they are the founders of the next version which is built differently. And that might be a bit whiplashy for people. I mean, I certainly hope that's true, it's certainly what people tell me. It's also what they appreciate about the company. It's like what is best ends up mattering a lot.
turns.zh: 我觉得托比龙卷风（Tobi tornado）就是把大量变革管理工作、沟通对话、冲突解决或坦诚交流浓缩到极短的时间里。我发现某个项目进展不顺……情况不妙时，我就去沟通。很快就能意识到：要么得更新原有认知，要么调整思路另辟蹊径。这时项目可能会暂停，我们会重新召集团队，启动新版本的开发。参与原项目的成员不再参与新版本的开发，而是成为新版本的创始人。这对有些人来说可能是个不小的冲击。但我真心希望这种机制能有效，因为很多员工都这么反馈，这也正是他们欣赏公司的地方。最终，真正有效的方案总能脱颖而出。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically, it's you going into a chat room being like "Hey, this" ... "We're going to end this project we're" ... "Let's try something else" because you've discovered or realized this is a bad idea. Some people complain about this practice of like "Oh, Tobi kills the we've been working on." My lens is, you realize we're just wasting time on this thing that is not going to work and we shouldn't do it. Is there anything there along those lines?
turns.zh: 简单来说，就是你走进聊天室，说：“嘿，这个项目……” “我们要结束这个项目……” “我们换个思路吧”，因为你发现或意识到这是个糟糕的想法。有些人抱怨这种做法，觉得“天哪，托比毁了我们一直努力的项目”。但我的看法是，当你意识到我们在浪费时间做根本行不通的事时，就应该及时止损。你们这边有没有类似的经历？

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: No. This is everything. Again, once I imagine something might be not the right thing to work on I'm either incorrect at which point this is super important that I understand why or I'm correct at which point it's super unfair for letting people work on something that isn't going to make it. There's a third wave which is I could also ignore it but that's an abjection of my CEO and founder responsibility that I'm absolutely not willing to make so that's just not a path forward that I see valid. I understand that's what a lot of people choose to do. So yeah, compressing time is important. We have a fairly limited time in our careers, right? Our careers are not that long. If you're lucky you have 40 years in the industry. Most people spent more time in school and then maybe leave later if they're so lucky that they can. So it's not even that. (00:07:33): I think you want to do the maximum amount of things you can be proud of at the end of your career. When you look back you want to be saying, "Hey, holy shit, we shipped this thing which was absolutely an incredible contribution to a mission I cared about at a company that was full of other people who cared as much as I did." And also are very proud of working. And maybe even thinking of working with me and being really, really glad that we spent time on projects together. Yeah, none of this happens if everyone's sort of optimizing a thing that probably shouldn't be there, right? And, therefore, I think it's the better thing to do.
turns.zh: 不是的。这就是全部了。再说一次，一旦我觉得某件事可能不值得去投入精力，我要么是判断错了（这种情况下理解原因至关重要），要么就是判断对了（但让人们去投入精力到注定失败的项目上，这太不公平了）。第三种情况是，我也可以选择忽视它，但那就是对首席执行官和创始人职责的背叛，我绝对不愿意这么做，所以我认为这条路走不通。我理解很多人选择这么做。所以没错，压缩时间很重要。我们职业生涯的时间毕竟有限，对吧？职业生涯本就不长。如果幸运的话，你能在行业里待40年。大多数人上学时间更长，如果足够幸运还能晚点离开职场。所以这不是关键。（00:07:33）我认为，你希望在职业生涯结束时，能做尽可能多让自己引以为傲的事。当回首往事时，你会感叹：“天哪，我们完成了这个项目，这对一项我深切关怀的使命做出了非凡贡献，而公司里还有一群和我一样充满热情的伙伴。”同时为自己的工作感到自豪。或许甚至会想起和我共事的时光，真心为能与我共事而感到庆幸。是啊，如果每个人都在优化那些本不该存在的东西，这一切都不会发生，对吧？因此，我认为这样做才是明智之选。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And, by the way, I love this way of describing ... Of compressing it in time to just make a decision, not focus on making it come across the most kind, nicest, sweetest way. When you give feedback to people when something is not the way that you think it could be or as good as you could be it's often very direct and often hard to hear. To me this comes across as you're trying to maximize their potential, you're trying to push them to do something better. Is there anything there that you think is a way of approaching feedback?
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我很欣赏这种用时间压缩来快速做决策的方式，不必非得用最委婉、最贴心的表达方式。当你给别人反馈时，指出某件事不符合你的预期或不够理想时，往往需要直言不讳，尽管这听起来可能刺耳。但在我看来，这恰恰是在最大化他们的潜力，促使他们做得更好。你觉得在反馈过程中有没有什么值得借鉴的方法？

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: I really, really, really think that there is not a single person on this planet who is even close to being at their maximum potential. I just think everyone is way, way, way, way, way better than they think. And the reason why we're not performing at this level is a series of ideas, maybe certain approaches for cultivating our skills and our crafts that have not yet been discovered and, therefore, we could not take advantage of them. It's an environment that just narrows the focus on fairly unambitious things at which point you get stuck competing with literally everyone else in the world because everyone's unambitious. (00:09:33): I have found that reminding people of their own potential constantly is actually a wonderful thing to do. And I have a history of being right about people's potential more than they are themselves. Now, in a way, this dooms me fairly often to be disappointed, right, in myself. By the way, I'm talking about myself here too. I think I have way more potential than what I bring to bear and I hate that so I'm trying to cultivate the skills that I need for tomorrow and constantly challenge myself. I'm harder on myself than on anyone else. By some discount rate act equally to the people around me, especially the ones who just so, obviously, are brilliant. (00:10:23): Spending time and longer time in careers with people and then holding them to a high standard means that they accomplish very often things that just they didn't imagine they could. To me this is the most wonderful thing to see. And frankly this is a throughline for all of my career because this ... My product is that. I want my product to cause people to be more successful than they thought they could. And, in fact, become more ambitious about what they are building with their online stores and their businesses than they are actually initially set out to do. (00:10:56): Because something like this happened to me, right? I started a snowboard store at some point. I didn't set out to build Shopify. If you are committed to following your curiosity as to the next step, and optimize for maximum amount of learning when you choose these steps, it takes you from one place to another and you actually realize the world's full of lies about human potential and progress. Maybe people are not malicious about it but they're definitely confused about it. School teaches you that you have to learn this particular piece of math in this 12 month period, and it doesn't matter how much you understand it. It's like the outcome can be variable and will grade you on a variable outcome for a fixed amount of time which has nothing to do with anything I've ever seen or learned or see ... Or witnessed about how to actually learn things. You follow that thread and you just find that there is no speed limit for personal growth. In a way Shopify has been a wonderful experimental lab for this sort of conviction. I've just seen this to come to be true. And, of course, hearing from someone that you respect that "Hey, I think you had it in you to do this thing significantly better because I think you probably saw fairly early in the project this sort of path A path B. You chose path B potentially out of convenience even though you knew that wasn't the right thing. And I actually expected better of you and I expected" ... "I think the next time this happens in your career you should go path A because" ... "Based on your conviction." And, therefore, that's hard to hear, right, because it's right. But it's also extremely valuable, right? What I love is an environment of people who are holding each other accountable to the actual potential rather than sort of their current level plus or ... Plus some, I don't know, a little bit extra.
turns.zh:
我真的、真的、真的认为，这个星球上没有一个人能完全发挥出自己的最大潜力。只是我觉得每个人都比自己想象的要优秀得多。我们之所以没有达到这种表现水平，是因为一系列尚未被发现的理念，或许是培养技能和精进技艺的方法，因此我们未能充分利用这些资源。这种环境只会把人们的关注点局限在一些平庸的目标上，最终你会发现自己在与全世界所有平庸之辈竞争，因为所有人都太缺乏雄心了。（00:09:33）：我发现，不断提醒人们意识到自己的潜力其实是一件很棒的事。就我个人而言，我对人们潜力的判断往往比他们自己还要准确。但某种程度上，这也让我经常对自己感到失望。顺便说一句，我这里说的也是我自己。我觉得自己的潜力远超目前展现出来的水平，我对此深感不满。因此，我正努力培养未来所需的技能，不断挑战自我。我对自己的要求比对任何人都严厉。我尽量以平等的标准要求身边的人，尤其是那些显然才华横溢的人。（00:10:23）：与职业生涯中的人共度更长时间，然后以高标准要求他们，往往会让他们实现超出想象的成果。对我来说，这是最美好的景象。坦白说，这贯穿了我的整个职业生涯，因为……我的产品就是要让人们比自己想象的更成功。事实上，让他们对通过网店和业务创造的成果抱有更高的雄心，远超最初的设想。（00:10:56）：因为类似的事情也发生在我身上。我曾开过一家滑雪板店，但我从未打算创立Shopify。如果你致力于追随自己的好奇心去探索下一步，并在选择这些步骤时优化学习效果，它会带你从一个地方走向另一个地方，最终你会意识到，关于人类潜力和进步，世间充斥着诸多谎言。或许人们并非故意为之，但他们肯定对此存在误解。学校教你必须在12个月内学完某门数学课，成绩如何并不重要。结果可能是浮动的，而评分依据的是固定时段内的浮动成绩，这与我所见所学、所目睹的真正学习方式毫无关联。沿着这条思路探索，你会发现个人成长没有速度限制。某种程度上，Shopify为这种信念提供了绝佳的实验场。我亲眼见证了这一切的成真。当然，当你尊敬的人对你说：“嘿，我觉得你本可以把这件事做得好得多，因为我在项目早期就看到了A路径和B路径。你选择了B路径，可能只是出于便利，尽管你知道那不是正确的选择。我原本对你有更高的期望，下次遇到这种情况，你应该选择A路径，因为……基于你的信念。”……这话听起来很难接受，因为它太对了。但这也极具价值，对吧？我所热爱的，是一个充满这样人的环境。
相互督促对方发挥出真正的潜力，而非仅仅局限于当前的水平，或者……再加上一些额外的努力，我也说不清，算是多加一把劲吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many threads I want to follow here. The example of the school is such a pertinent one. To me right now we're looking at preschools for our son and I'm ... They're describing their education philosophy I'm like, I don't know why I should believe this is the right approach. And it makes me just want to spend all this time researching what education approach works. I know it's just preschool and maybe not as critical yet.
turns.zh: 啊，这里有太多我想关注的讨论了。学校这个例子特别贴切。就拿我们现在为儿子挑选幼儿园来说，我真是...他们在讲教育理念时，我总觉得自己没理由相信这就是正确的路径。这让我忍不住想花大量时间研究哪种教育方式更有效。虽然只是幼儿园阶段，或许还不是至关重要的。

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: Did you have a bet yet? I have three kids too and this is sort of a decision that every parent faces, right? So many of your listeners are probably product managers of machine learning products that maybe this resonates. So there's a funny thing about machine learning which you're just like ... You train on a lot of data, and, hopefully, you get something that predicts the thing you want it to predict correctly out of it. The biggest problem of this is overfitting, right? What does good look like, a loss function? Which is a heuristic because it's not the actual task that the thing will do in the future it's something that proxies to the task that you want the thing to do in the future. Predict fraud, predict the next word, whatever. So overfitting is basically model learning how to cheat on the benchmark or on the fitness function. (00:14:39): So there's a business analogy of this which is that ... It's called Goodhart's law. It's literally the same thing as overfitting just for businesses. Goodhart's law just says, "Any metric that becomes a goal ceases to be a good metric." Same exact thing. The universal truths are things that almost any competitive field will invent for itself by different terminology often. And I think this is also, by the way, why it's so interesting to focus on personal growth and learning a lot about a lot because you end up finding these sort of hidden harmonies behind things, the things that are clearly enduring correct insights. So overfitting, Goodhart's law are the same thing. School optimizes for what? Marks supposedly, right? In fact, overfitting in school is literally the kids cheating to get marks, right? You get another analogy. What is however the right loss function for children? Have you made a decision yet?
turns.zh: 你下注了吗？我也有三个孩子，这几乎是每个家长都要面对的决策，对吧？很多听众可能是机器学习产品的PM，所以这个话题应该能引起共鸣。说到机器学习，有个很有趣的现象——你用大量数据训练模型，期望它能准确预测目标结果。但最大的问题是过拟合，对吧？什么样的结果才算优秀？损失函数就是个启发式指标，它并非模型未来实际执行任务的标准，而是替代性地衡量你期望它完成的任务，比如预测欺诈、下一个单词等等。过拟合本质上就是模型学会了如何在基准或适应度函数上作弊。（00:14:39）这和商业领域的古德哈特定律如出一辙——任何成为目标的指标都不再是好指标了。核心道理完全相同。通用真理往往是各个竞争领域通过不同术语重新发明的东西。比如专注个人成长、广泛学习新知，你就能发现事物背后隐藏的共鸣，那些经得起时间考验的真知灼见。过拟合和古德哈特定律本质相同。学校优化什么？表面上是成绩，但实际是孩子们为了成绩作弊，对吧？这又引出另一个类比。那么对孩子来说，正确的损失函数是什么？你做决定了吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I have not we just started down this path. You told me-
turns.zh: 没有，我们才刚开始考虑这个问题。你之前跟我说...

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: It's the kind of thing [inaudible 00:15:57]. You have to actually go fairly deep in philosophy to figure this out. And then again afterwards you can build, you can find the schools that you like. For us it was just maintaining curiosity. This is a completely different goal from being good at marks. But I just think everyone's born extremely curious and school has a habit of getting it out of kids. Literally, there's a foundation model of a child, and you fine-tune it at school, and it just loses the neurons of curiosity because it's actually discouraged to meander into other topics and explore them just because they're interesting. I don't know. This is sort of not the beat of a podcast but I just think about this a lot. It's funny how these things just recur constantly.
turns.zh: 这类问题需要深入思考哲学层面的东西。之后再根据这些思考来选择学校。对我们来说，关键是保持好奇心。这和追求高分完全是不同目标。但我觉得每个人天生就极具好奇心，学校却总有办法磨灭这种天性。字面上说，孩子有一种基础模型，学校会对其进行微调，但最终好奇心的“神经元”会被消磨，因为探索其他有趣领域的能力被压制了。我不知道。这或许不该是播客的主题，但我对此思考良多。这些现象反复出现，实在耐人寻味。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So when Archie was on the podcast, he's the head of growth at Shopify ... I don't know if that's his official role. Basically drives a lot of the growth. He talked about how the core product team, outside of the growth team, operates without KPIs, without specific goals. And decisions are driven by taste and intuition primarily you, and Glen, and some other leaders. And a lot of people heard that and they're like "I" ... "First, I don't believe that. Second of all, how does one operate that way when there's no data to tell us exactly what is right and good?" So the question I have is just how does one operate in that way successfully? What does it take for a company to work that way because a lot of people will try it and fail?
turns.zh: 阿奇做客播客时透露，他是Shopify的增长部门主管……虽然我不确定这是否是他的正式职位，但他确实主导了公司的大部分增长战略。他谈到，除增长团队外，核心产品团队在运营时并不设定KPI（关键绩效指标）或具体目标，决策主要基于个人判断和直觉——比如你、格伦以及其他高管的判断。许多听众听后纷纷质疑：“第一，我不相信这种说法；第二，既然没有数据来明确判定何为正确之举，那该如何运作呢？” 所以我真正想问的是：如何才能成功地以这种方式运营公司？一家企业要想实现这种运作模式，需要具备哪些条件？毕竟，许多尝试这种模式的公司最终都以失败告终。

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: This is very close to what I just talked about before with [inaudible 00:17:28]. Goodhart's law is real. The moment a metric becomes a goal it's no longer a useful metric, right? I think that's more or less a precise wording. Why? Because no metric by itself is a complete heuristic for a complex business because business are complex. There's a million of different tensions in a company and you can't all keep them in harmony by optimizing for one fix. It's true that we don't have KPIs and we don't have at least OKRs in the Silicon Valley sense but we are extremely data-informed. We have invested enormous amounts of money and time into systems that give us basically everything at our fingertips. I sent this demo to other founders and they're completely bowled over by the way we can dig into basically every constituent atomic bit part that makes up the cohort that just got formed 15 minutes ago by the end of a ... At the end of a quarter or month or week. (00:18:39): In a lot of different places, this is one of them but also in its products, it's just not overfitting for the quantifiable. Everyone competes for everything but it's highly quantifiable because it's ... It's fun, it's like a game. You tweak a number and 0.1 more is better than 0.1 less. That's an immediate gratification thing. But I just think the overlap of most valuable things you can do with a product, and for things that happen to be fully quantifiable, it's like maybe 20% which leaves 80% of a value space unaddressable by the people who will only look at quantifiable things. Shopify is comfortable with the unquantifiable things such as tastes, quality, passion, love, hate. It's with the strong emotions that people have. (00:19:49): The sort of deep satisfaction that a craftsperson feels when they've done a job well is actually better proxy if you allow it to be then the ... Do a unit test pass. A unit tests might not pass. And the unit tests will pass 15 minutes later because we already fix them or adjust the one or two things so they support us. We have systems that tell us exactly if something goes the wrong way. There's an extremely sophisticated rollout system in Shopify that forever holdouts and correlates everything with everything for ... In every experiment and so on and so on and so on. But if you think about it as a cockpit for a pilot. The decisions are still made by pilots and we think this leads to better results. It's just the same with our product. There's plenty of A/B testing tools and all these things for commerce, and it's, of course, really important to figure out what your conversion rates are. But are you representing your brand is an unquantifiable question? Are you proud of the thing that you have built? Do you feel it's your own, right? (00:21:03): And so I think there needs to be more acceptance in businesses or for unquantifiable things. The most powerful, not unquantifiable things in the world of business are fun and delight. If people have fun when they're doing something that is just upstream from so ... Sorry, downstream from so many other things. I think that if all the metrics are pointing down but everyone says, "My God, I'm having so much more fun," I think that the very next thing that will happen with some time delay is all metrics will start going up. And if that doesn't happen then we adjust course. (00:21:51): The reason why we specifically don't have OKRs and these things is because ... If you want to hold the unquantifiable as things that are stable and exist ... That people actually do really defer to them and really actually learn to be okay with someone just saying, "Hey, this is actually just really great and they're shipping this" then you need to make certain edits to a business that don't remind everyone too much of the companies they might have come from which the only way to get promoted is by driving the metric up. It's a bit of a [inaudible 00:22:24] conversation I suppose. Good on the fortune cookies saying, "Shopify doesn't do OKRs or doesn't do metrics" and so on. But it's actually just because the metrics take us [inaudible 00:22:37] function where we often defer to just more ... Sometimes a little bit emotional but generally less quantifiable things.
turns.zh:
这和我们之前讨论的古德哈特定律很相似。（00:17:28）当一个指标成为目标时，它就不再是一个有用的指标了，对吧？我觉得这句话说得很到位。为什么呢？因为没有任何单一指标本身就能为复杂的商业环境提供完整的决策依据，毕竟商业本质上是复杂的。公司内部存在无数相互矛盾的诉求，你不可能通过优化某个单一指标就让所有矛盾和谐共处。确实，我们在硅谷没有KPI或OKR，但我们对数据的依赖程度极高。我们投入了大量资金和时间开发系统，几乎能随时获取所有关键信息。我把这个演示发给其他创始人，他们对我们能深入分析15分钟前刚组建的用户群组的每个微观细节感到惊叹——无论是按季度、月度还是周度追踪。（00:18:39）在很多领域，包括产品开发中，人们往往过度关注可量化指标。但这种量化思维其实存在过拟合的风险。所有人都争相追逐量化指标，因为量化容易量化，就像玩游戏一样——调整一个数字，稍微高一点就比低一点好，这能带来即时满足感。但我认为，一个产品中最有价值的部分和可量化指标的重叠度可能只有20%，这意味着80%的价值空间无法被只关注量化指标的人所触及。Shopify乐于接受不可量化的东西，比如品味、质量、激情、爱恨等强烈情感。（00:19:49）工匠完成工作时获得的深切满足感，如果能被视为一种更有效的衡量标准，那比通过单元测试通过更重要。单元测试可能没通过，但15分钟后就会通过，因为我们修复了问题或调整了参数。我们的系统能准确告知问题出在哪里。Shopify有一套极其复杂的上线系统，不断追踪和关联所有数据，进行反复实验。但如果把这比作飞行员的驾驶舱，决策最终还是由飞行员做出。我们认为这种方式能带来更好的结果。我们的产品也是如此。市场上有大量A/B测试工具，但关键在于转化率。可你的品牌代表性如何？你为自己打造的东西感到自豪吗？你觉得这是属于自己的成果，对吧？（00:21:03）所以我认为企业需要更包容不可量化的东西。商业世界中最强大的非量化因素是乐趣和愉悦。如果人们在做某件事时感到开心——哪怕这件事处于其他许多事情的上游——我相信只要所有指标都在下滑，但大家都说：“天哪，我现在开心多了”，接下来很可能所有指标都会回升。如果没有这种效果，我们就调整方向。（00:21:51）我们特意不采用OKR等工具的原因是……如果你想把不可量化的东西当作稳定存在、人们真正依赖的存在……那人们真的会重视它们，真正依赖它们。
学会坦然接受别人说"嘿，这其实太棒了，他们在搞CP"。然后，你需要对业务进行一些调整，避免让大家过多联想到他们之前待过的公司——毕竟在那种公司里，唯一的晋升途径就是把各项指标往上拉。这算是一场有点难以启齿的对话吧。我倒挺欣赏那些福袋上写着"Shopify不搞OKR，不搞KPI"之类的话。但其实这只是因为那些指标把我们带入了一个误区，让我们往往更倾向于……有时甚至带点情绪化的东西，但总体来说更难量化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine if someone were to hear you describe this of focus on joy, and fun, and love, and delight, maybe ... It's easy to dismiss that.
turns.zh: 我想，如果有人听你描述这种专注于快乐、乐趣、爱和喜悦的生活方式，也许……人们很容易对此不屑一顾。

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: It sounds completely idiotic, right? Again, there's an aesthetic in the world that exists which is that business people dress in suit and tie, they are speaking much more sophisticated than I do usually without an accent, have a full head of hair. They talk about metrics, they are in front of PowerPoint presentations, they usually have a stick and show dramatically at the pie chart that is behind them. And highly charismatic, highly ... So that's our aesthetic. How much is that aesthetic overlapped with our performance? I don't know but some of them ... Some people pull it off who are like this. I think the world is sort of stacked to lead us astray based on our stories about what optimal looks like are just so incorrect in so many ways. Optimism always sounds dumb, or at least naive. Pessimism sounds extremely sophisticated. Metrics driven sounds extremely sophisticated. Talking about fun sounds like naive. (00:24:14): Well, first of all, I've always ignored what people think generally. That came pretty natively to me somehow which I'm very lucky about. But I've now actually learned that almost all of the alpha in the world is now in the ... Exactly the things that are unobvious but true. And the things that people dismiss as naive or so. The most successful business person on planet Earth is Elon and he conforms to no idea of what the most sophisticated business person ought to be like in any which way you can imagine. I think we live in a world where the counterfactuals are winning because our ... Because aesthetics are just leading us astray.
turns.zh: 这听起来简直愚蠢至极，对吧？再说了，这个世界存在着一种审美标准——商界人士身着西装打着领带，言辞精妙得体，没有口音，满头秀发。他们谈论着各种数据指标，站在幻灯片前，手持教鞭在身后展示饼状图，还要极具魅力……这就是我们所认同的审美标准。但这种审美标准与我们的实际表现又有多大关联呢？我不知道，但有些人确实能做到。比如我认识的某些人就做得很成功。我认为这个世界在很多方面都误导了我们，让我们对理想状态的定义产生了严重偏差。乐观主义总是显得愚蠢，或者至少显得天真。悲观主义则显得极其深邃。以数据为导向的思维方式也显得极其高明。谈论乐趣则显得天真。（00:24:14）：首先，我向来无视大众的看法。这或许是我与生俱来的幸运之处。但现在我发现，世界上绝大多数的优势都来自那些看似不明显却真实存在的事物，以及那些被人们视为天真或幼稚的事物。地球上最成功的商人是埃隆，而他在任何方面都与人们对最成功商人的刻板印象相去甚远。我认为我们生活在一个反事实占上风的世界，因为审美标准正在误导我们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is an awesome segue to the other theme that I wanted to spend some time on which is thinking from first principles, Elon is the classic example of that. Honestly, I think you're the other most classic example of that these days. And we'll keep talking about all the ways you operate very differently from other companies which are examples of this. But I want to read a quote from Glen Coates, he shared with me, of how he sees you that gives an interesting lens into your first principles thinking. So here's what he said about you. "Tobi is at his heart a true futurist, he's obsessed with the way things should be in the future. Being data-driven is innately being anchored in the way users and technology are behaving today. He's never really said this to me explicitly, but knowing him I think any design that is drawn primarily from the way things are or were is one that he sees as inferior to one that is skating to the puck of the way things could or should be." Does that resonate?
turns.zh: 这为我接下来想深入探讨的另一个主题——从第一性原理思考问题——提供了一个绝佳的过渡。埃隆就是这方面的典型例子。说实话，我认为你也是当今最典型的例子。我们会继续探讨你与其他公司截然不同的运营方式，但我想先读一读格伦·科茨分享的关于你的评价，这为你的第一性原理思维提供了有趣的视角。以下是他对你的评价：“托比本质上是一位真正的未来主义者，他痴迷于未来应有的样子。数据驱动本质上就是基于用户和技术当前行为方式的锚定。他从未明确跟我说过这些，但据我了解，任何主要基于现状或过去的思维方式的设计，在他看来都比不上那些朝着未来可能或应该的样子前进的设计。” 这让你有共鸣吗？

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think that's correct. That's actually really interesting. Your podcast is a podcast by a-
turns.zh: 是的。我认为这很准确。这真的很有意思。你的播客是一档由——

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: Your podcast is a podcast by a builder for other builders. Here's the most interesting question I think people can ask builders is like, "What is your energy source? Where are you getting energy from?" I think fundamentally the world exists at room temperature. Almost all companies are running at that, humming along, doesn't do anything. There are certain individuals who can inject heat into businesses. Founders do this very well. All the startups anyone's ever heard of have people who are injecting heat because if no one would inject heat into the business, at room temperature, you cannot outperform anyone else. You can't be hotter than everyone else if no one's injecting heat into the concern. So fundamentally, there is a injection of energy into companies that comes from founders and the best leaders, like all the people you've had on the podcast from Shopify have a perfect set of cast of characters of people who are just exothermic. They are just like wellsprings of energy that leads to all the amazing results that we get to enjoy. (00:27:21): So the question is where does energy comes from? And that's another one of our discussions which very quickly goes into the emotions. Actually, there's a really... So I watched The Last Dance, the Netflix special of Michael Jordan a while ago, of course, but there was one scene where he just, I'm sure this is a super famous story and he just made up an insight that someone told him so that he would then go and just want to destroy them afterwards, which he then of course proceeded to do because it's hard to imagine anyone more exothermic than him. So we know what his energy source is. It's rivalry. It's potentially it's insight or it's anger, something like this. (00:28:06): I am not... My energy source is dissatisfaction with status quo. My fundamental belief is all this talk about technology where all... So many books are about just technology leading to dystopia. You know what dystopia is? Today, compared to what it will be in 20 years ago or any. And you can play this for any part of human history. I'm not making a future statement. I'm making a almost totalical statement about the experience on planet Earth. No one who really thinks about this would want to be born into a world 20 years before today rather than today. And so I think today is the dystopia of future, and I think it behooves us to try to build the kinds of products that lead in towards progress in a small way or a big way. But yes, I think if someone comes to me and says, "Hey, let's go do this thing. And we've looked around and here's how people solve this problem, let's make a good version of that," I'm like, "That was not the job." Because everything that you encounter, that every solution, every product, everything that exists is path-dependent, highly, highly, highly path-dependent, and often path-dependent based on having to make compromises, based on things that were true at the time a decision was made but are no longer true. (00:29:38): The entire field of... What was it? I forgot the name of a field. Chomsky's field, the linguistic research field. It's cool. We now have autoregressive models that are just like, we don't actually need to set up a complete... We don't need to research the structure of grammar to be able to make machines also engage in the spoken word. We actually can just train on the internet, it turns out. So that was not possible back then because you didn't have the right architecture for this, but now it is. So I think what you have to do is to actually have, when you come up with a new product or you discuss a new product, you have to derive it from first principles. You have to say, "How would we solve this problem given every fundamental building block that we have available right now?" (00:30:25): For that, to do that, you actually have to understand the power and the composability of all the building blocks that exist right now, which is a tall order and no one is perfect at this. But so this way, you go ahead and say, "Okay, cool, so this is how we are implementing this thing. This is how it will be implemented today." And now we can talk ourselves in taking shortcuts. "Maybe we should actually start up doing it the way everyone else does. Maybe we derived exactly what everyone else does as the correct thing to do." (00:30:56): Sometimes there was a lot more wisdom encoded in the status quo than you expect, which is I think is super delightful. Then you figure that out and so when you act on it. But what isn't okay is skipping the exercise and doing the same thing everyone else does because that is again a abdication of product leadership. And so yeah, I would say I become extremely suspicious if I get a pitch to do a good version of the same thing everyone else does because I just find that in our space specifically very rarely to be the best solution.
turns.zh:
你的播客是为建筑者打造的播客，供其他建筑者聆听。我认为人们能向建筑者提出的最有趣的问题是：“你的能量来源是什么？你从哪里获取能量？” 我认为从根本上说，世界在室温下运行。几乎所有公司都在这种状态下运转，平稳前行，却毫无作为。只有某些人能为企业注入热量。创始人最擅长这一点——所有我们耳熟能详的初创公司背后，都有注入热量的人物。如果没有人为企业注入热量，企业就会停滞不前。既然没有人注入热量，你就无法超越竞争对手。于是，创始人和顶级领导者为企业注入能量，这正是播客中嘉宾如Shopify团队所展现的特质——他们都是充满能量的源泉，推动着我们所享有的惊人成果。（00:27:21）那么，能量从何而来？这也是我们探讨的另一个核心议题，很快就会涉及情感层面。说到这，我最近看了网飞纪录片《最后的舞者》——关于迈克尔·乔丹的故事。其中有个场景：乔丹肯定听过一个故事，但随口编造了一个洞见，之后就想亲自去击败对手。最终他也确实做到了，因为很难想象还有比他更能量的存在。由此可见，乔丹的能量来源是竞争。可能还有洞见或愤怒之类的因素。（00:28:06）我不这么认为——我的能量来源是对现状的不满。我的核心观点是，所有关于技术的讨论，太多书籍都把技术描绘成通向反乌托邦的途径。你知道什么是反乌托邦吗？今天的世界与20年后或更久后的世界相比，是天壤之别。这种对比适用于人类历史的任何阶段。我不是在预言未来，而是对地球现状的观察。没有一个真正思考过这些问题的人，会希望出生在20年前的世界，而不是今天的世界。因此，我认为今天就是未来的反乌托邦。我们有责任尽力打造能推动进步的产品，无论是微小进步还是巨大突破。但如果有人对我说：“嘿，我们来做这个项目吧。我们研究了现有解决方案，现在要做出更好的版本。”我会说：“这不是我的任务。” 因为你遇到的每种解决方案、每款产品、每种存在的事物，都高度依赖于发展路径，往往基于当时的决策而产生的妥协，基于当时正确但如今已不再适用的假设。（00:29:38）整个领域……叫什么来着？我忘了那个领域的名字。乔姆斯基的领域，语言研究领域。很酷。我们现在有了自回归模型，不需要构建完整的语法结构，就能让机器理解口语。事实证明，这在过去是不可能的，因为当时缺乏合适的架构，但现在已经可以实现了。所以关键在于，当你提出新想法时，必须真正具备……
无论你是在设计一款新产品，还是讨论一款新产品，都必须从第一性原理出发。你必须问自己：“鉴于我们现有的所有基础构件，我们该如何解决这个问题？”（00:30:25）要做到这一点，你必须真正理解现有所有构件的强大功能和可组合性。这是一项艰巨的任务，没有人能做到完美。但这样一来，你就能继续说：“好的，很棒，所以我们就是这样实现这个功能的。这就是我们今天要实现的方式。” 而现在，我们可能会想当然地说：“或许我们应该效仿别人的做法。或许我们得出的结论和别人认为的正确做法一模一样。” （00:30:56）有时，现状中蕴含的智慧远超你的想象，这真的很令人欣喜。当你发现这一点并据此行动时，那再好不过。但不可以做的是跳过这个思考过程，直接模仿别人的做法，因为这又是对产品领导力的放弃。所以，如果有人向我提议做一个别人都做过但做得更好的版本，我会非常怀疑，因为在我们这个领域，这种做法很少能成为最佳解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple quotes along these lines I've seen that describe the way you think about this stuff. "If most people are doing it a certain way, I, by default, don't want to do it that way. And if you want to do something world-class, you can't do it like everyone else."
turns.zh: 我见过不少类似的引语，描述了人们看待这类问题的方式。比如：“如果大多数人都在用某种方式做事，那我默认就不想用这种方式。如果你想做出一流的东西，就不能跟其他人做得一样。”

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: Yeah. I don't even think that's an opinion that I hold. I think that's actually... We are basically in axiom territory here. If you want to do something better than what exists, you have to do it differently. That does not make a statement about if it will be better in the end after you do it. It could also be worse. But you can't get something better done if you do the same thing. It's like axiomatically not possible to do. It's fails Archimedean logic, yet it's something... You would be amazed how many business plans are actually failing Archimedean logic in this way like, "Let's do a good version of this thing that we've already been doing and we will capture 1% of the market," and just like this stuff. It's like, "Trust me." I find it kind of cute.
turns.zh: 是啊。我甚至不认为这是我个人的观点。我觉得这其实……我们这里基本上涉及到一个公理层面的问题。如果你想做得比现有水平更好，那就必须另辟蹊径。但这并不能保证你最终就能做得更好。结果可能更糟。但如果你还是沿袭老路，就不可能做得更好。这种做法从公理层面来看就是不可行的。它违背了阿基米德逻辑，却又……你会惊讶于有多少商业计划都是这样违背阿基米德逻辑的，比如“我们把已经在做的事做得更好，就能占据1%的市场份额”之类的。这就像在说“相信我”。我觉得这挺有趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example that you can share of you approaching the problem this way? I imagine it's constantly happening. You also mentioned you're born this way. So I think it's hard for someone to just sit down, learn, think the way Tobi thinks, but I'd love to help people start to approach problems this way, so maybe an example might help.
turns.zh: 你能举个例子，说明你是如何用这种方式解决问题的吗？我想这种情况肯定经常发生。你还提到自己天生就这样。所以我觉得，要让人静下心来学习，培养出托比这种思维方式确实很难，但我很乐意帮助人们开始用这种方式解决问题，也许举个例子会有帮助。

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: I think this is entirely learnable, I think. And so I encourage people to just have a practice of think step by step essentially and just do it. It'll become a habit pretty quickly because it just, it also just outperforms. (00:33:09): Examples. The very first example is Shopify itself. It's cool. So there was lots of e-commerce software and it was all the way it was because of path dependence because everyone who want it in 2004, 2005, e-commerce was an existing retailer and therefore they had complex businesses that needed to be ported online, including all of their somewhat Byzantine business logic. "I wanted to make e-commerce software that would do very well on the internet of the future and I believe that we can make it easier to start new businesses online than it is in a physical world because the physical world is encumbered by a lot of regulations and also upfront costs for leases and so on. So let's optimize for that case and build something that is so intuitive to use that frustrated people in dead-end careers can spend their lunch breaks making progress towards building their own business, which then eventually allows them to do it on their own way." (00:34:25): And so being fortune was biased, eventually it turns out to be a much better prep for also solving all the enterprise cases because no one had to... Enterprise software is overfit to the sales process, which is that it wins the RFPs because it has every feature ever or at least a way of putting a checkbox next to every RFP line ever. But they're not good, right? An RFP is a great example of overfitting in the world of procurement because it tells you nothing about the quality of software behind it. But honestly, this happens all the time. It is just like here, we are setting the stage for much more, much higher quality retrieval for the products on Shopify and across Shopify. I think we've been in a local maxima on search and we think that, especially with the advances of the new models, certain things are now possible to do that could not have been done yet because again of these layers and layers of path dependence and no one coming and saying, "Is that the best way to do and maybe we should rebuild this component periodically?" We can now do a better job if search that will leads to much more delightful experiences. And so this is a fun project that this happening right now in.
turns.zh: 我认为这完全是可以学习的，我觉得。所以我鼓励人们养成一种习惯，就是一步步思考，然后就去做。这很快就会成为一种习惯，因为它确实表现出色。（00:33:09）：举例来说，第一个例子就是Shopify本身。它很棒。当时有很多电商软件，但它们之所以存在，是因为路径依赖。2004年、2005年，想要做电商的都是现有零售商，他们的业务复杂，需要迁移到线上，这包括他们那些相当复杂的业务逻辑。“我想开发一款能在未来互联网环境下表现出色的电商软件。我相信我们能让在线创业比实体创业更容易，因为实体世界受制于诸多法规，以及前期租赁等成本。所以让我们针对这种情况进行优化，打造一个易于使用的平台，让那些陷入职业瓶颈的人能利用午休时间推进创业，最终实现自主创业。”（00:34:25）：Shopify的成功并非偶然，最终它为解决所有企业级问题做了更好的铺垫，因为企业软件往往过度适应销售流程。比如，它能赢得RFP（招标书），因为它把每个RFP条款都涵盖进去，功能繁杂却不实用。这就是路径依赖的典型例子——RFP无法反映软件的实际质量。但这种情况太常见了。我们现在正为Shopify及其他平台上的产品打造更优质的搜索引擎。我认为我们在搜索领域曾陷入局部最优，尤其随着新模型的进步，某些原本无法实现的功能现在变得可能。这是因为层层路径依赖阻碍了创新，也没人停下来反思：“这真是最佳方案吗？或许我们该定期重建某个组件？”现在我们能做得更好，让搜索体验更令人愉悦。这是个当前正在推进的有趣项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is really interesting because what I'm looking for is like the Tobi algorithm of first principles thinking. Elon's got these famous ways of thinking he shared. One is start with the cost of metal to help you understand how much a rocket should cost. And then he's got this five-step. First, decide, do we need this thing? Then figure out how to optimize it, then automate it. What I'm hearing so far, and I'm curious if you've thought about this? And if not, this feels like a really good blog post in your futures, the Tobi first principles algorithm, but I'll share a couple of things I've heard so far as you've described it. (00:36:24): One is analyze the path that existing solution has relied on, almost like the assumptions that were true for it to be built back and it was built. And the other is this overfit, what is it overfit for? What is it over solving that maybe isn't necessary? Is there anything along those lines of just how you approach problems?
turns.zh:
我觉得这很有意思，因为我一直在寻找类似托比算法的基本原理思维。埃隆分享过一些著名的思考方式。比如，用金属成本估算火箭成本。还有五步法则：先判断是否需要，再优化，再自动化。到目前为止，我听到了很多观点，不知道你是否考虑过这些？如果没有的话，这听起来像是在你博客里写一篇很棒的文章——托比基本原理算法。不过我还是想分享一下你提到的几个观点。
（00:36:24）：一个是分析现有解决方案依赖的路径，类似于构建该解决方案所依赖的假设。另一个是过度适应的问题，过度适应什么？可能有些过度解决的需求其实没必要？有没有类似的方法来处理问题？

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: This is probably too nerdy technical. You are right, but I should figure myself out a little bit. My brain runs on a meter language but isn't directly something I can translate into words, I suppose. I think more about things like this in terms of programming constructs, pure functions, overstate. And I think in any moment, the best decision to do is I think the perfect product lead is almost like a thermostat for high quality product. It's like you're setting, saying, "I would like to build something really, really great and I'm going to go through a series which is much, much more complex than what a thermostat does," which basically checks the temperature and then makes a decision of air con or heating. You make you re-derive literally every decision that is valuable, every foundational assumption, every foundational ABC direction. And you want to see the observation you've made in the meantime since you last derived the next step. Re-running the entire function over the state that is now updated, the higher fidelity information, would you come to the very same thing? (00:38:08): Sometimes fairly early in the construct in the tree of foundational assumptions, change is made. An example we all had was beginning of COVID when we suddenly had shelter in place. So Shopify has that incredibly good office spaces and we were very in-person company and we've... Our floor plans because I think we really added something to the understanding of how to put great... I got a lot of founder energy from my co-founder, Daniel, to build great collaborative spaces for creative work with lots of happy accidents, people running into each other and so on. (00:38:46): Anyway, we were very, very, very, very determined on doing that. But somewhere in this construct of nesting functions, you have to rerun and foundational assumptions. It's in the stack is the fairly basic Boolean of are people allowed to leave a house? Which was yes. The moment that flips, it's not that just like, "Okay, over here let's do the best what we can do." It's actually that the entire tree now moves into a different place. And it can be a very far place, different, that you land because you will make the same quality of decision on every step, but you need to rerun something that takes you to a completely different landing zone. And so then this is also easy for us to say, "Cool, we are going to be remote only forever? Let's go." And because we realized that the temporal shelter in place would cause a series of events that would make that for optimal best set of trade-offs for the company. And so I think this is... Can I put this into a piffy five-step? I wouldn't know, but maybe it resonates with someone who can help me figure out the coded English language for this because it has been nerdy way the I explained it, even to me.
turns.zh: 这可能太书生气、太技术化了。你说得对，但我确实需要好好反思一下。我的大脑用的是一种隐喻语言，但又不是能直接翻译成文字的，我觉得。我更多地会用编程结构、纯函数、过度设计之类的术语来思考这类问题。在任何时刻，最明智的决策或许就是，产品负责人几乎就像一个调控高品质产品的恒温器。就像你设定一个目标，说：“我想打造一款真正出色的产品，我要经历一个比恒温器复杂得多的过程。”恒温器只是检测温度，然后决定是开空调还是暖气。对于每一个有价值的决策、每一个基础假设、每一个基础ABC方向，你都需要重新推导。同时，要回顾自上次推导下一步以来你所观察到的变化。重新运行整个函数，基于更新后的状态和更高精度的信息，你是否会得出同样的结论？（00:38:08）：有时，基础假设树中的某个层级很早就发生了变化。比如新冠疫情初期，我们突然实施居家令。Shopify拥有极好的办公空间，而我们原本是一个高度聚集的公司。我们……我们的楼层规划让我对如何打造出色的……我从联合创始人丹尼尔那里获得了大量创业能量，共同打造了适合创意工作的协作空间，充满了意外的灵感，比如员工们不经意的碰撞等等。（00:38:46）：总之，我们当时下定决心要做到这一点。但在层层嵌套的函数结构中，你必须重新审视基础假设。比如关于人们是否被允许出门的那个基本布尔值，之前是允许的。当这个条件反转时，整个决策树就必须转向一个完全不同的方向。可能这个方向会非常遥远、截然不同，但只要每一步的决策质量不变，你最终会到达完全不同的落脚点。于是我们轻易地就决定：“好吧，我们永远只远程办公？开始吧。”因为我们意识到，临时居家令会引发一系列事件，最终为公司带来最优的权衡平衡。所以我觉得……我能不能把这总结成五个步骤？我不知道，但也许有人能帮我把这段复杂的英文翻译成通俗易懂的中文，毕竟我自己解释得太书生气了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This remote work example is something I definitely wanted to touch on, which is I'm glad you got there. So in this decision, is there anything more you could share about how you got to that place of like, "Oh this Boolean changed so we should rethink this?" Because I know you probably, you weren't... I don't know. Were you in the shower and just like, "Oh wow, we should really go remote because of this"? How did that actually come about? And then I wanted to ask on another part-
turns.zh: 这个远程工作的例子是我特别想探讨的，很高兴你提到了这一点。在这个决策过程中，关于如何意识到“哦，这个布尔值变了，我们得重新思考”，你能否再分享一下？因为我知道你可能……我不知道。你是不是在洗澡时突然灵光一闪：“哇，因为这个我们应该转为远程办公！”具体是如何发生的？然后我想问另一个问题——

turns.speaker: Tobi Lütke
turns.en: Yeah, pretty much actually yes because again, I rerun over all the inputs and figure out what happens. And here's a couple of other things that were starting to fray on the decision to be in person as well. We started in Ottawa, Canada, which is a city of a million people, and it has some tech heritage and good universities. But at a million people, it's just not population dense enough and has a depth of talent pool that it can support a company that is going to 10,000 people. So anyone who runs this optimization function I'm talking about here about location strategy for a new startup will come to the conclusion if they do it right that everyone should be sitting around the same table. Only if you can't do that, do you say, "Okay, let's be all in the same couple of rooms." Only if that doesn't work anymore, you say, "Okay, let's be spread over one floor." If that doesn't work, in the same building. If that doesn't work, in the same city. If that doesn't work, at least stay in the same time zones or make sure that there's good hub connections between. (00:41:39): This is how it works. It's just like some assumption somewhere along the line is invalidated. You end up in a different side of a decision tree. But what was happening to us was we already were in four or five cities. We were adhering to the same time zone at this point. But my experience was I went through, sometimes at the Ottawa office, through an entire day where I had 10 hours of meetings, which is fairly normal, but I do every single... I don't think I had a single other person sometimes with me because every one of them was with people in another office. Some people are dialing in remote and so on. So there was an awkward hybrid-ness which we ended up in making only good decisions along the way. (00:42:29): This is actually the most dangerous thing. Most of the time you end up in a bad part of a tree, in a local maxima of a path-dependent environment, by only making good choices. People think that making a good choice inoculates you from making mistakes or that the presence of a downside of an idea ends up disqualifying the idea. Both of those things are incorrect. So what you need to do then is... So that was an overlay to decision. (00:42:59): The moment COVID started, then we also had this thing of shoppers exploding because we were actually an asset to people during COVID, e-commerce for the local businesses. And we took that very, very seriously trying to make more businesses survive COVID, small businesses survive this particular calamity than otherwise won't which is important because small businesses tend to be wiped out first anytime the times turn fragile. And so we needed to staff up. And so there's a very weird question about where to staff up. So clearly the better input there would be if you could hire people everywhere. And so once that decision flipped, you can see how this is actually now super easy to say, "We are going to remote," because there is no turning back. There is no... Even with this decision, it's a better set of trade-offs for the future is to accept the vast additional difficulty of building a remote company. It's way harder. (00:44:03): It's not something you should recommend to anyone to do this because it's the same as trying to run a world record marathon run in Aspen, Colorado. It's like there's not enough oxygen up there to do that. But if you end up pulling it off, you're a real Chad. That's very cool. So I find difficulty itself interesting. And again, I spent enough of my teenage years on the internet to know that there's amazing cultures that can be put together purely remote like, I don't know, Wikipedia, World of Warcraft, Raiding Guilds can at least have excellent cultures. And so we are like, "Okay, cool. Let's come to a new stable part." That stable part was don't port the office online. Let's port the internet into a company and then we are like, "Let's go."
turns.zh:
是的，实际上确实如此。因为我再次检查了所有输入数据，分析了可能的结果。还有其他几个因素也让线下办公的决定变得越来越困难。我们最初在加拿大渥太华开展业务，那里有百万人口，拥有一定的科技底蕴和优质大学资源。但百万人口的城市人口密度不足，无法支撑一个发展至万人的公司所需的人才储备。因此，任何负责新创公司选址策略优化的人，如果能正确规划，都应该让所有团队成员集中在同一办公场所。只有当这不可行时，才考虑分散在同一楼层的办公室。如果这也不行，就选择同一栋楼内的不同楼层。如果还是不行，至少要确保在同一时区内，或确保各办公点之间有良好的交通连接。（00:41:39）这就是整个决策过程的逻辑。某个环节的假设一旦失效，就会将你引向决策树的不同分支。但我们当时已经在四五个城市开展业务，并且统一了时区标准。但我的亲身经历是，有时在渥太华办公室，我会经历一整天的会议——这很正常，但几乎每次会议都没有其他同事参与，因为每个人都在与其他办公室的人开会。有些人通过远程会议参与等等。这种尴尬的混合办公模式最终导致我们只能做出权宜之计。（00:42:29）这实际上是最危险的情况。大多数时候，你会因为只做出明智决策而陷入局部最优陷阱，认为做出一个好决定就能避免犯错，或者认为一个想法的负面影响就足以否定其可行性。这两种观点都是错误的。所以你需要做的是……这就是决策过程中的一个附加考量。（00:42:59）新冠疫情爆发后，我们还面临着用户激增的挑战，因为我们在疫情期间为本地商家提供了电商服务，成为了他们的重要支持平台。我们非常认真地对待这项工作，努力帮助更多小企业渡过难关。毕竟，小企业往往最先在经济环境恶化时倒闭。因此，我们需要扩充团队。这就带来了一个奇怪的选址问题。如果能在各地招人，显然是最优的选择。一旦这个决策确定，就很容易说出“我们将转为远程办公”了，因为没有回头路了。即便做出这个决定，从长远来看接受远程办公的巨大挑战也是更明智的权衡。毕竟远程办公要难得多得多。（00:44:03）我不建议任何人尝试这种模式，因为这就像在科罗拉多州阿斯本尝试跑马拉松——那里氧气不足，根本无法完成。但如果你最终成功了，那你就是个真正的猛男，非常酷。所以我觉得困难本身就很有趣。再说，我青少年时期在网上泡得够久，知道
令人惊叹的文化能在完全远程的情况下汇聚在一起。比如，我不知道，维基百科、魔兽世界、攻城公会至少都拥有卓越的文化。因此我们会想：“好吧，不错。让我们进入一个新的稳定阶段。”那个稳定阶段就是不把办公室搬到线上，而是把互联网引入公司，然后我们就开始行动了。
